quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While hiking back from a peak at dusk, your buddy pair realizes you missed a trail junction and are no longer sure where the main trail is. Following the BSA S.T.O.P. survival protocol, what should you do?
options: Run downhill through the woods before total darkness falls to look for a road.
Stop immediately in place, Think calmly without panic, Observe your surroundings/weather/daylight/gear, and Plan shelter and signaling while staying together so searchers can find you.
Split up and hike in opposite directions to cover twice as much ground.
quiz_item.correct_answer: Option B — Apply S.T.O.P. (Stop, Think, Observe, Plan), stay together in one visible location, prepare shelter before dark, and use 3-blast whistle signals.
quiz_item.explanation: Moving randomly after losing the trail increases search radius exponentially and risks injury after dark; staying put with S.T.O.P., shelter, and 3-signal distress calls maximizes rapid rescue.

pamphlet_excerpts: Flash Lightreflected Signal: When the sun is shining, the flash of lightreflected with a signal mirror can be seen for miles.
Sight Target Hole: Sight a target through the hole in the center ofthe mirror or by looking just over the mirror’s top edge.
Night Flashlight Send: At night, use a flashlight to send groups of three flashesin the direction where you believe rescuers might be able tosee them.
Flares Airplanes: Flares can be found on airplanes and in some watercraftand motor vehicles and can be effective if you have a rescueaircraft in sight.
step_by_step_procedure: They Visible Short: They are visible for only a short time, though, so save them for the right moment.
Hanging Brightly Colored: Hanging brightly colored clothing or camping gear on tree branches can catch the rescuers’ attention.
Flags Banners Contrasting: Flags, banners, and contrasting colors can be part of your signaling efforts.
Wave Shirt Yourhead: If you can see rescuers, wave a shirt over yourhead or attach it to a pole and wave it as a flag.

pamphlet_excerpts: Drink Water It bears repeating: Drink plenty of water.
Survive Days Without: You can survive for days without food, but inhot weather without water, only hours.
Dehydration Happens Cold: Dehydration happens in cold weather, too, even though you may not feel as thirsty.
Thebest Rule Drink: Thebest rule is to drink plenty of water, enoughso that your urine is clear, whenever you arein the outdoors.
step_by_step_procedure: Ideally Waterwhere Lake: Ideally you will be able to find waterwhere you are, from a lake, a stream, or melting snow, or by guiding rainwater down a tarp or tent fly.
Watermay Collected: Watermay have collected in depressions in rocks, inthe crotches of trees, or in seeps along cliffs.
Surest Means Water: The surest means of making your water safe is byboiling it.
Pot Metal Container: Use a pot or other metal container on a stove orover a fire and bring the water to a full boil.

requirements.req_text: Careers. Do ONE of the following: (a) Explore careers related to this merit badge. Research one career to learn about the training and education needed, costs, job prospects, salary, job duties, and career advancement. With permission of your parent or guardian, your research methods may include an internet or library search, an interview with a professional in the field, or a visit to a location where people in this career work. Discuss with your counselor both your findings and what about this profession might make it an interesting career. (b) Explore how you could use knowledge and skills from the Wilderness Survival merit badge to pursue a hobby or to serve as volunteer. Research any training needed, expenses, and organizations that promote or support it. Discuss with your counselor what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursue this.
